text.p: Troops loyal to Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen have consolidated their control of major towns after Sunday's ouster of First Prime Minister Prime Norodom Ranariddh, drawing condemnation from the United States.
Members of the royal family and leading officials Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party took the chance on Wednesday to flee the fighting.
Here are some key facts about Cambodia, a constitutional monarchy with an elected government and parliament:

POPULATION: An estimated 10.5 million. Ethnic Khmers (Cambodians) account for 90 percent of the population, which includes sizeable minorities of Moslem Chams, Chinese, Vietnamese and hill tribes. Theravada Buddhism is the state religion.
AREA: 181,035 square km (69,898 sq miles) of which about 40 percent is forest. Neighbours are Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.
CAPITAL: Phnom Penh, population before the fighting started estimated at 900,000.
ARMED FORCES: The armed forces gather members of the three major parties that formed a coalition government in 1993 and numbers have been swollen by Khmer Rouge defectors.
Army -- An estimated 140,000 soldiers with artillery, armoured personnel carriers and about 100 tanks.
Navy -- 7,000-8,000 men with some 35 vessels for coastal and riverine patrols and 100 smaller boats. The navy headquarters is near Phnom Penh on the Mekong River and has a coastal base at Ream.
Air Force -- 2,000 men with about 40 modern and ancient aircraft, including helicopters, L39 trainer jets and four MiG-21 interceptors under renovation.

Some 10,000-15,000 Khmer Rouge guerrillas have defected to the Cambodian armed forces since August 1996. Four former rebel commanders have been appointed two-star generals and 15 made one-star generals.

ECONOMY: The Cambodian economy relies predominantly on agriculture, though light industry and tourism continue to grow. The industrial sector gained a boost in 1996 with the granting of Most Favoured Nation trading status and the government is hoping to win Generalised System of Preferences privileges. The garment industry has seen rapid growth but was hit by unprecedented labour disputes in early 1997.

The Cambodian parliament approved a budget of 1.5 trillion riel ($556 million) for 1997, with about a quarter going to defence. Foreign assistance continues to account for about 40 percent of the budget.

The government banned timber exports from December 31, 1996, in response to criticism of forestry policies and rampant logging. The IMF cut a $20 million loan in 1996 because of the government's lack of transparency in accounting for logging revenues.

Per capita gross domestic product in 1996 was less than $300 and growth of around six percent was forecast. Year-end inflation was estimated at about seven percent. Cambodia's currency, the riel, fell slightly in value over 1996 and was trading at around 2,700 to the dollar.

HISTORY: The great 9th-15th Century Angkor empire once ruled most of Southeast Asia from the site of modern-day Siem Reap province in northwest Cambodia, but the country subsequently came under the alternating sway of neighbouring Thailand and Vietnam.
France ruled Cambodia as a protectorate from 1863 to 1953, when King Norodom Sihanouk led the country into independence at the start of a relatively golden era.
Sihanouk, who had abdicated in 1955 to conventrate on politics, was overthrown in a 1970 coup that signalled the start of civil war.

The Maoist Khmer Rouge guerrilla movement toppled the U.S.-backed Lon Nol republic in April 1975 and launched a brutal rule of almost four years under the notorious Pol Pot which left more than one million people dead from execution, disease, starvation or overwork in vast agricultural labour camps.

Vietnamese troops invaded Cambodia in 1978 and installed a friendly socialist government that was not shunned by the Western world and which faced a three-party resistance coalition, nominally led by Sihanouk but spearheaded by the Khmer Rouge.
Rival factions signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact in 1991, which culminated two years later in general elections and restoration of the monarchy with Sihanouk on the throne.
A coalition, spearheaded by the royalist FUNCINPEC and formerly communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP), was formed but tension flared in 1996 over power-sharing.
The Khmer Rouge began to fracture in August 1996, when former top cadre Ieng Sary split with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot.
Thousands of guerrillas joined the government over the following months, but celebrations were dampened when FUNCINPEC and the CPP began vying for allegiance of the defectors.

Fighting began in the capital on Saturday, ignited after Second Prime Minister and CPP leader Hun Sen ordered a crackdown on "illegal troops" under the command of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh who also heads FUNCINPEC.

Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh as his forces took control of the capital and major cities. According to preliminary reports, 58 people died and almost 200 were wounded in the weekend fighting in Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen's troops on Monday arrested Ho Sak, top FUNCINPEC official, and later shot him dead, an interior ministry official said.
The United States condemned the violence and on Wednesday said it was withdrawing 40 diplomats but leaving its mission open.

Members of the royal family fled the country and Cambodia's Southweast Asian neighbours started evacuating their nationals. Cambodia's U.N. ambassador said Ranariddh's supporters would amass troops in the second city of Battambang and set up and alternative regime.
Members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) were due to meet on Thursday to consider whether or not to postpone Cambodia's entry into the bloc, originally planned for this month.
